Who sends the Akron tax bill

Akron is inside Summit County, so your bill comes from the county's Fiscal Office. One elected fiscal officer oversees three divisions. Valuation sits with the Auditor, payment and collection with the Treasurer, and deed filing with the Recorder. You will deal with the Auditor over a value dispute, the Treasurer over payments, and the Recorder at the sale.

The office moved to a temporary location during the renovation of its usual building. Look up the counter address on the fiscal office website before driving down.

Second-half deadline and penalty

Real estate tax here is split into two payments, and the later one closes in July. The 2025 second-half cycle ran late, with bills starting to go out June 24, 2026 and the last day to pay falling on July 31, 2026. The fiscal office blamed Ohio House Bill 186, a law that added an Inflation Cap Credit for some school districts sitting on the 20-mill floor and for joint vocational districts on the 2-mill floor, and that forced a one-time rate recalculation. Expect timing to shift again whenever the state changes the rules, so confirm the current closing date with the Treasurer Division.

A mailed check needs a U.S. postmark dated no later than the due date, or the statutory 10 percent penalty applies. Stamps from a private postage meter are rejected. The law makes the owner responsible for getting the bill. When nothing arrives, phone 330-643-2588 and request a duplicate, since a missing envelope is no excuse.

Ways to pay an Akron tax bill

Pick whichever of these suits you:

  • Walk in to the Treasurer Division counter.
  • By mail, following the postmark rule above.
  • Pay by phone or web with ACI Payments. Cards carry a service fee and e-checks cost $1. Keep the parcel number handy.
  • At participating banks in the Regional Tax Collection System. The branch must be in Summit County, and not every bank takes cash.

If you cannot pay a whole half at once, the Tax Installment Program is open to owner-occupied parcels with everything current. Enroll at (330) 643-2869. A second option, the Real Estate Discount program, takes monthly coupon payments toward a half and credits you with a return tied to county investment yield. Sign up July 1 to October 31 for the first half or January 1 to March 31 for the second, with taxes current. Military reservists on active duty can defer taxes by calling (330) 643-2641.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Selling with delinquent taxes

A Delinquent Tax Payment Plan, running since 1987, gives owners who skipped either half a way to pay in monthly installments. After enrollment the overdue balance moves into a separate account that stops collecting interest, and the added interest is wiped out once you finish the plan. Current-year bills must still be paid on time. The Delinquent Tax Department is at 330-643-2600.

The county can sell a tax certificate lien on an unpaid parcel. Paying in full or arranging a plan stops that, and sale fees and costs may land on the owner. Ask the Treasurer Division for a payoff figure ahead of closing so the title company can build it into the numbers. Lenders and cash buyers alike expect the balance cleared, so request the figure early.

Appealing your Akron valuation

Value complaints go to the Board of Revision. File between January 1 and March 31 by postmarked U.S. Mail, at the counter, or in the Smartfile online system. Questions go to bor@summitoh.net or 330-926-2559.

  • Three officials sit on the board: the fiscal officer, the county executive and the clerk of courts, or their stand-ins.
  • A complaint begins a legal proceeding. You must prove your number with documents.
  • Only the valuation is open to challenge, not the tax bill.

Counties reappraise every six years and update values in the third year. New construction is added at cost. Replacing a roof does not push the appraisal up, though structural work on wiring, plumbing, framing or the foundation can. Bring photos, repair bids and nearby sale prices.

Homestead exemption and owner-occupancy credit

Homestead takes the first $29,000 of appraised value off the taxable base for a single-family home and saves $535 a year on average. People with a 100 percent service-connected disability rating get a larger exemption on the first $58,000. Applicants who are over 65 or permanently and totally disabled need household income under $40,000 for 2025 applications and $41,000 for 2026. Call (330) 643-2661 with questions.

A separate owner-occupancy credit trims the tax from qualified levies on your main home. Apply by December 31 of the year you become eligible. Rentals do not qualify, and the credit stops when the home is sold or no longer your residence. Ask the fiscal office which credits sit on your parcel before you list.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Transfer and recording fees when you sell

Transfers are cleared by the Property Transfer Department, which checks the legal description and conveyance. Sellers file DTE Form 100, the statement of value and receipt, or DTE Form 100 (EX) when the transfer is exempt. Complete forms turned in by 3:30 p.m. can transfer title the same day, per ORC 319.202 and 319.54(G)(3).

Summit County Fiscal Office fees for a property transfer
ChargeAmount
Conveyance fee$4.00 per $1000, rounded up to the next $100 of the sale price
Lot fee50 cents per lot in the legal description, exempt or not
Basic recording$34.00 for 2 pages, $8.00 each added page
Non-compliant document$20.00 per document
Cross reference$4.00 each

The purchase contract decides who covers each charge. Your title company can show the split on the settlement statement.

A seller's checklist for Akron

Start by asking the Treasurer Division whether anything is owed on the parcel, including a half you have not yet paid. If you are behind, enroll in the payment plan or pay it off, and get a payoff figure in writing for the title company. Then confirm with the fiscal office which credits and exemptions are attached to the parcel, since a buyer's statement of value can ask about them.

Before the closing date, have DTE Form 100 prepared and ready, and aim to get it in by 3:30 p.m. if you want title to transfer the same day. Expect conveyance, lot and recording charges on the settlement statement. A cash buyer skips the lender's payoff and appraisal steps, but the county's forms and fees do not change.

Akron housing at a glance

Akron's population was 189,691 in July 2025. Only 50.7 percent of homes are lived in by their owners, against 67.5 percent across the county. Median owner-occupied value is $122,000 versus $208,700 countywide, and median gross rent is $955. Since roughly half the housing is rented, a seller with a tenant should sort out the lease before listing.

Frequently asked questions

Where do Akron tax payments go?

To the county Treasurer Division. Akron does not bill separately.

When is the second-half Akron property tax due?

July. A mailed payment needs a postmark on or before that day or the 10 percent penalty applies, so call the Treasurer Division for the exact date.

What is the Akron complaint window for value?

January 1 through March 31, by mail, in person or in Smartfile. The Board of Revision answers questions at 330-926-2559.

What does the Akron conveyance fee run?

It is $4.00 per $1000 of price, with the price rounded up to the next $100, and 50 cents for every lot in the legal description.

Can I catch up on overdue Akron tax?

Yes. Phone the Delinquent Tax Department at 330-643-2600 about the payment plan. It freezes the overdue balance with no new interest while you pay monthly and stay current.

Cincinnati, OH Property Tax Guide: Offices, Dates and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in Ohio
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Cincinnati, OH Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Cincinnati, OH Property Tax Guide sale
  • Turn the Cincinnati, OH Property Tax Guide offer down and you owe us nothing

Owe Cincinnati Property Tax? Get a Cash Offer

We buy Cincinnati houses as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Behind on Cincinnati property tax?

Who taxes and bills a Cincinnati house

The city of Cincinnati does not send a property tax bill. Hamilton County does. Two county offices handle it. The auditor decides what each parcel is worth, and the treasurer mails the bills and collects. You will find the treasurer's staff in Room 402, 138 East Court Street, or reach them at 513-946-4800 on weekdays from 8 to 4.

A three-person Board of Revision hears value disputes. Its seats belong to the auditor, the treasurer and the commissioners' president. The city levies tax and gets its share of the proceeds, but it never values or bills your house.

Due dates and penalties

Expect two bills a year. For 2026 the first half went out in mid-January with a February deadline, while the second half was mailed in early July and due in late July. The second pair of dates was moved late because state legislation requiring an Inflation Cap Credit forced the treasurer to recalculate second-half bills. Dates can shift in other years, so read the deadline printed on your bill.

  • A payment that comes in during the ten days after the deadline carries a 5 percent penalty. Later than that, the penalty is 10 percent.
  • To ask for a penalty to be reviewed, download the Penalty Remit Application from the treasurer's site.
  • No discount is given for paying early, but a prepayment plan named TOP lets owners pay ahead in installments.

How to pay

There are four ways to pay.

  • Online through Point & Pay. The vendor, not the county, charges $1.00 for an eCheck or 2.35 percent on a credit card.
  • By phone to the same vendor at 1-877-764-3524.
  • By mail, with a personal check, cashier's check or money order made out to Hamilton County Treasurer. Write the stub or parcel number on the memo line.
  • At the Room 402 counter, the only place that takes cash.

Mail counts as on time when postmarked by the due date. Trouble is, the Postal Service postmark reflects when a machine sorts the envelope, possibly after the day you dropped it off. When the deadline is close, give the envelope to a clerk and request a hand stamp.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What goes into the bill

The county taxes 35 percent of market value, called assessed value, and states every rate in mills, where a mill means $1 for each $1,000 of assessed value. Voted levies are tempered by a reduction factor so they stay close to what voters approved, even as values climb. Then the state subtracts credits: non-business for residential property, owner occupancy, and homestead.

Your bill shows the county levies below plus separate lines for school district, township and city or village. Great Oaks career campus levies apply in every Hamilton County school district except Cincinnati and Northwest.

Selected Hamilton County levies
LevyMillsTerm
County general fund2.26Continuing
Public library2.501.00 expires tax year 2027, 1.50 expires 2033
Developmental disabilities4.13Expires tax year 2028
Park district1.980.03 continuing, 0.95 expires 2030
Crime information center0.54Continuing
Zoological park0.46Expires tax year 2027

Look up your own district's total rate in the treasurer's Rate of Taxation download.

Challenging your value

Owners who believe the market value is too high can file a complaint with the Board of Revision from January 1 through March 31. Call the board at 513-946-4035 and find forms on its website. The cutoff under section 5715.19 is March 31 following the tax year, or the close of first-half collection when that comes later. A postmark on or before that day saves a mailed filing.

A complaint can attack market value and nothing else, because local levies are not open to challenge. Until the board rules, you are allowed to pay on the lower value your complaint claims.

Delinquent taxes

Once a payment is missed, penalties and interest begin to build. A phone call to 513-946-4800 can set up a delinquent contract that breaks past-due amounts into scheduled payments, as long as new bills are paid on time. While the contract stays in good standing, the house is shielded from added penalties, interest, foreclosure and a lien sale.

  • Balances left after second-half collection are certified delinquent that November. They can enter a lien sale the following October, usually near mid-month.
  • Eligible liens are sold to financial institutions in one negotiated block, not one by one to individuals, and extra fees attach once a lien is sold.
  • A tax foreclosure is a lawsuit filed by the county prosecutor. Owners typically get 28 days to answer the summons, and a judgment leads to an online sheriff's sale.
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Homestead and other credits

Ohio's homestead exemption reaches Cincinnati owners through the county auditor. The 2026 credit covers the tax on $29,700 of value for qualifying seniors and disabled owners whose income is within $41,000. Disabled owners who are former service members get the tax on $59,400 of value, with no income test.

One credit takes no paperwork: the stadium sales tax credit goes automatically to owners who already receive the 2.5 percent rollback on an owner-occupied home. Homestead forms, however, are due December 31 of the year you want the credit.

Cincinnati as a selling market

The city is made of 52 neighborhoods on hills and ridges. Three places, Norwood, Elmwood Place and St. Bernard, are enclaves with their own governments, so check which jurisdiction a street belongs to. The July 2025 population estimate is 314,367, owners hold 39.8 percent of homes, and the typical owner's home is worth $230,900. With under four in ten homes owner-occupied, many sellers are landlords or heirs, and each parcel's tax status should be checked separately.

Selling with taxes owed

Unpaid tax stays with the parcel, and a title search will find it. Request a payoff figure from the treasurer that includes earlier years and hand it to the closing agent. If the lien has already been sold, the treasurer can name the buyer of the lien, and your payoff will include that holder's added fees.

An owner who is behind but wants to keep the house can sign a delinquent contract before the lien sale, which keeps the parcel out of it as long as current taxes are paid. A cash buyer can close quickly, provided the title company pays the tax balance out of your proceeds at the table. Bring your latest bill and parcel number to the closing, and ask the title agent to confirm in writing that nothing remains owed.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

What number reaches the office that sends Cincinnati tax bills?

Dial 513-946-4800 for the Hamilton County Treasurer, open weekdays. Value questions go to the Board of Revision at 513-946-4035.

When is the second-half Cincinnati bill due?

In the 2026 cycle it was due in late July, after a late change caused by the Inflation Cap Credit. Dates can differ in other years, so check the printed bill.

What penalty applies to a late Cincinnati property tax payment?

Five percent during the first ten days after the due date, then 10 percent. A Penalty Remit Application is available on the treasurer's site.

What is the filing window for a Cincinnati value complaint?

January 1 through March 31. The complaint goes to the Hamilton County Board of Revision, and mail postmarked by March 31 counts.

Can unpaid taxes cost me my Cincinnati house?

Only through foreclosure. A lien sale moves the lien, not the house, and the holder may start foreclosure after a year. A delinquent contract signed before the sale, with current taxes paid, keeps the parcel off the list.

Cleveland, OH Property Tax Guide: Offices, Dates and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in Ohio
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Cleveland, OH Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Cleveland, OH Property Tax Guide sale
  • Turn the Cleveland, OH Property Tax Guide offer down and you owe us nothing

Owe Cleveland Property Tax? Get a Cash Offer

We buy Cleveland houses as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Behind on Cleveland property tax?
We buy Cleveland houses as-is, and the title company pays unpaid tax from the proceeds.
Get My Cash Offer →

Who values and bills a Cleveland house

Cleveland city hall plays no part in billing real estate tax. Cuyahoga County does the work: its Fiscal Officer sets each parcel's appraisal, and its Treasurer sends the bills and takes payment.

You will find both at 2079 East 9th Street, Cleveland, Ohio 44115, in the county Administrative Building. The cashier is on the first floor, appraisal on the third, and Transfer and Recording on the fourth. The Treasurer's taxpayer line is 216-443-7400, option 1. MyPlace, the county's online property search, lets you pull up a parcel and view its taxes.

Four things build a bill: the millage in your taxing district, any special assessments, the property's value, and reduction credits such as owner occupancy and homestead. The Board of Revision hears challenges to value only. The Treasurer publishes residential and commercial rates for each community, so check the taxing district on your bill before comparing a Cleveland house with one in a suburb.

Cleveland housing snapshot

The city lies on Lake Erie's southern shore, and the Cuyahoga River divides it into an East Side and a West Side across 34 neighborhoods. The population estimate for July 2025 is 363,608, down from 372,635 in April 2020. Roughly 41.7 percent of homes are owner-occupied. A typical owner-occupied home is valued at $102,000, rent at the median is $945, and household income at the median is $40,801, across 169,683 households of about 2.09 people. Rentals make up most of the stock, so the registration and disclosure rules below reach a large share of sales.

Due dates, penalties and how to pay

Two installments are billed each year, due in February and August. Shortly after each deadline a 10% penalty is assessed. Delinquent prior-year tax picks up 9% interest on September 1 and another 3% on December 1. The county bills in arrears, so tax due in 2026 is for tax year 2025. Manufactured homes follow their own calendar, with the current year's tax due in early March and late August.

Ways to pay Cuyahoga County property tax
Payment methodCost and instructions
OnlineNo fee for e-check; $2.95 flat for debit; 2.3% for credit, $1.50 minimum.
Phone1-877-738-1212, entering an asterisk wherever the parcel number has a space.
MailCuyahoga County Treasurer, PO Box 94547, Cleveland, OH 44101
In person or drop box2079 East 9th Street. Satellite locations open only during the January and February and July and August collection seasons.

A mailed postmark shows when the sorting machine handled the envelope, so send early or have a clerk hand-stamp it.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Appealing your valuation

Complaints about value are accepted January 1 through March 31, and a weekend deadline rolls to the next business day. The board prefers its e-file portal, which asks only for an email address and phone number and skips the notary. On paper, deliver to 2079 East 9th Street, 2nd Floor, or fax 216-443-8282, between 8:30 a.m. and 4:30 p.m.

The board encourages the state's DTE 1 form. Question 9 wants your opinion of value as one exact number, and a blank or a range gets the complaint dismissed. You must prove your number, so bring a recent sale price, a listing agreement from the past three years, an appraisal or repair estimates. By mail, the complaint needs a United States Postal Service postmark dated March 31 or earlier; a courier's private meter mark is rejected. Rates, levies and penalties are beyond the board's power.

What the city requires before closing

Under section 367.12 of the city code, a seller or transferor of real property must give the buyer a Certificate of Disclosure. The application lists a $60 fee for each structure on the lot, filed by the escrow or transferring agent on the city's online portal.

City staff fill in Part F of the form, which covers the lot's legal use, the number of structures, a Certificate of Occupancy where it applies, any historic district status, any condemnation or open violation, and lead hazard control orders. When violations are open, the buyer signs the notice and attaches it to the purchase agreement. The form also asks whether the house is a rental with a current registration and, for rentals built before 1978, a lead safe certificate.

  • Anyone who buys to rent must register the address with Building and Housing once the deed transfers.
  • A house left empty goes on the Vacant Property Registry within 15 days after the transfer.
  • Rental registration costs $70 per unit, renewed yearly, with renewals opening after January 1 and payment due by March 31.

An owner who lives beyond Cuyahoga and the neighboring counties must name a Local Agent in Charge, and a building with four or more rental units also needs a heating system inspection certificate.

Behind on property tax

Current tax unpaid ten calendar days past the close of collection draws a 10% penalty. Older delinquent tax runs at 12% a year, and continued nonpayment can end in tax foreclosure and a sheriff's sale.

The first tool is a payment plan. Bring photo ID and a voided check or bank statement for automatic monthly deductions, and certified funds if the parcel is in foreclosure or a tax lien. The current year's tax must be paid on time as well, and while a plan is active the parcel is not offered at a tax certificate sale or by the sheriff. The Treasurer holds Last Chance Payment Plan classes for owners seeking a third contract. Residents 67 and older earning under $70,000 may qualify for a separate Taxpayer Assistance Program.

Cleveland's residential tax abatement program, run under Ordinance 482-2022 since January 1, 2024, offers 85% to 100% of the increased assessed taxes on permitted improvements, with single-family abatement possibly capped at home values between $350,000 and $450,000. If you rehabilitated a house with a city permit, ask the county whether an abatement attaches to the parcel and for how long it runs.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Recording a Cleveland deed

Transfer and Recording, at 216-443-2060, takes new recordings until 4:00 p.m., half an hour before the rest of the office closes. Every transfer needs a DTE 100 Statement of Value and Receipt, or a DTE 100-EX when an exemption from the conveyance fee applies. The recording fee is $39 for the first two pages and $8 for each page after that. County staff cannot give legal advice, and the Ohio Supreme Court treats drafting a deed as the practice of law.

The Fiscal Officer also offers Property Alerts, which notify an owner about potentially fraudulent filings against real property, and a Great Estates Program with guidance on avoiding unnecessary cost and delay in settling an estate. Owners who inherited a Cleveland house may find that second program useful before listing.

Selling a Cleveland house with taxes owed

Unpaid tax stays on the parcel until paid, so a buyer's title search will find it. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff figure, and have the title company pay it from your proceeds at closing. A cash buyer can close quickly, but the Certificate of Disclosure, the DTE 100 form and the payoff all still come first. Start the city disclosure application early, since open violations or a missing rental registration can slow the file.

Frequently asked questions

Which office do I pay for a Cleveland property tax bill?

Pay the Cuyahoga County Treasurer, not the City of Cleveland. Options are online, by phone at 1-877-738-1212, by mail to PO Box 94547, in person at 2079 East 9th Street, or through the drop box there.

When is the Cleveland valuation complaint deadline?

March 31, or the next business day if it falls on a weekend. The window opens January 1, and the Board of Revision prefers e-filing on form DTE 1.

What is the Cleveland Certificate of Disclosure?

It is a city document required when a house is sold or transferred, with a listed fee of $60 per structure. It tells the buyer about open violations, condemnation history, rental registration and lead-safe status.

What does Cleveland charge to register a rental?

The city charges $70 per unit for non-owner-occupied residential property. It is renewed yearly, and fees are due by March 31.

What interest does Cuyahoga County charge on delinquent tax?

Delinquent real estate tax carries 12% a year, charged as 9% on September 1 and 3% on December 1. A 10% penalty applies to late current payments.

Billing and valuation offices

Columbus city hall sends no property tax bill; the county does. Franklin County's Treasurer prints and collects it, and the Franklin County Auditor produces the valuation behind it. Part of Columbus spills into Delaware and Fairfield counties, so an address along the northern or southern fringe may answer to a different auditor and treasurer. Find the county named on your latest bill first, then make your calls.

OfficeWhat it handlesPhone and address
Franklin County AuditorValues, tax reduction applications, the Board of RevisionBoard of Revision: 614-525-3913, 373 S. High St., 20th Floor
Franklin County TreasurerMailing bills, collecting payments, penalties614-525-3438, 373 S. High St., 17th Floor, weekdays 8:00 to 5:00

Every tax year moves through the same sequence. Levies go to voters in November, the Board of Elections certifies the vote, rates get settled between the Auditor and the Ohio Department of Taxation in early December, and bills go out by mail later that month. The county tax list holds 440,173 parcels, and 239,956 of them are paid by a mortgage servicer, so plenty of owners never open a paper bill. In that case, ask the servicer for the figures before you list the house, because buyers like to see actual numbers.

Due dates and penalties

Columbus owners pay a year behind. Tax year 2025 was collected in 2026, with the second half due July 20. The first half lands in late winter. The county shifted its due dates in 2026 without touching the amount owed, so go by the date printed on your own bill and not by last year's calendar.

Options include one lump sum, two halves, or monthly installments, and about 171,000 parcels use the monthly budget plan. Escrow is the owner's responsibility even when a lender handles the money, so make sure the lender's account lines up with the new dates. The Treasurer accepts mail, walk-in and online payments. A payment plan or delinquent tax contract you already have stays in force as agreed when dates move, and money paid early is credited to the account in the normal way.

Miss a deadline and ORC 323.121 adds a penalty of ten percent on the unpaid part of that half. Settle the whole amount within ten days and the penalty is cut in half. Never getting a bill does not excuse the penalty. If one has not arrived, phone 614-525-3438 and ask for the amount. It also pays to confirm the Treasurer has your current mailing address after a move.

Because the county bills a year behind, a bill that arrives after you sell can still cover months you owned the house. Ask the closing agent how the year is being split, and keep a copy of the settlement statement showing what was paid on your behalf. If you sell to a cash buyer on a short timeline, call the Treasurer early in the process so the payoff is ready before the closing date is set.

How to appeal your valuation

The tool is form DTE 1, a Complaint Against the Valuation of Real Property, filed with the Franklin County Board of Revision. This season ends March 31, 2027, and the board accepts complaints from mid-November through March 31 each year. A residential complaint comes with a Residential Data Sheet. For form questions, call the board at 614-525-3913.

Ohio reappraises every six years and updates at the halfway point. Outside those years, your value shifts only if the building is altered or torn down, or the board orders it. Evidence carries the day here. Photos of defects, an appraisal or recent nearby sales will help far more than a hunch that the number looks high.

If you win, here is how the money moves:

  • The board's decision opens a 30-day appeal window, and refund processing starts once it closes.
  • Expect the refund roughly three weeks after that, not counting mail time.
  • The refund goes to whoever paid the tax, which may be a mortgage or title company instead of you.
  • If the house has changed hands, any tax still owed on it is deducted before a refund is cut.
  • A payment made after its due date sits in the Treasurer's surplus account until the owner asks for its release.
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Homestead and other tax reductions

The Auditor runs a handful of reduction programs, and every one has its own state form. Those that can apply to a Columbus house:

  • Homestead exemption for senior citizens, disabled persons and surviving spouses, form DTE 105A
  • Homestead exemption for an owner holding a total disability rating from military service, form DTE 105I
  • Owner-occupancy reduction, form DTE 105C, for a home that was the owner's primary residence when the tax year began
  • Reduction for storm or fire damage, form DTE 26
  • Current agricultural use value, form DTE 109, meant for working farmland and a poor fit for a city lot

Before listing, learn whether your parcel carries any of these. The value statement a buyer files under ORC 319.202 puts the question to the seller directly, and a yes has to be dealt with at closing. The new owner may not qualify for the same break, so the bill can climb after the sale.

Who handles the tax bill at a Columbus closing?

The title company or closing agent does. The Auditor stays out of closings and prorates nothing. The agent divides the tax year between you and the buyer and pays what is due from the proceeds. To keep that smooth, work through these steps before closing day:

  • Get a payoff figure from the Franklin County Treasurer.
  • Check the parcel for a delinquency or tax contract and tell the agent what needs clearing.
  • Mention any open Board of Revision case, since a recent sale can complicate a refund.
  • Make sure the Treasurer's mailing address is current, so the next bill finds the new owner or lender.

At transfer the seller owes the auditor's conveyance fee under ORC 319.54, which is $1 or ten cents per hundred dollars of value, whichever is greater, plus any county transfer tax. After that the auditor puts the parcel in the buyer's name. A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting, yet the payoff and the conveyance fee are handled the same way.

Columbus housing snapshot

Columbus is home to roughly 938,396 people as of July 2025, which is 3.6% above its 2020 count. A typical owned home is valued at $252,900 for 2020 through 2024. Just 44.1% of homes are owner-occupied, so renters make up the majority, and median gross rent is $1,295 a month. Those are citywide figures, and one block can sit far from them. To price a particular address, get a written offer or a local appraisal, and have your latest tax bill on hand.

Frequently asked questions

Which county bills property tax for my Columbus house?

Usually Franklin County, but parts of Columbus lie in Delaware and Fairfield counties. Check the last bill to see which county treasurer sent it.

When are Franklin County real estate taxes due?

The second half is due July 20. The first half comes due in late winter, and its exact date is printed on your bill.

Can I appeal my Columbus property value?

Yes. File form DTE 1 with the Franklin County Board of Revision before the season closes on March 31, 2027. The board's number is 614-525-3913.

Does the county prorate taxes when I sell?

No. The Auditor takes no part in closings. The title company or closing agent splits the bill between buyer and seller.

What if I never received a tax bill?

The tax is still owed and a penalty can still apply. Call the Treasurer at 614-525-3438 to get the amount.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326

Who bills and who values a Dayton house

Dayton does not collect property tax itself, even though the city is where the county seat sits. Montgomery County handles it with two offices: one sets the value of your house, and the other sends the bill and takes the payment. Billing questions go to Taxpayer Services at 937-225-4010, option 1. Value questions go to the auditor at 937-225-4326.

QuestionWhere to goPhone
Reading or paying a billMontgomery County Treasurer, Taxpayer Services937-225-4010, option 1
Behind on taxes, payment plansTreasurer, delinquency specialist937-225-4010, option 2
Value, levies, tax increase questionsMontgomery County Auditor937-225-4326
Valuation complaint formAuditor's Board of Revision937-496-6856
Solid waste charge on the billSemi-Annual Property Charge line937-224-8463

The treasurer collects on more than 250,000 real estate parcels, which is why phone, online and drop box options all exist. Pick whichever suits you, but keep a record of the date and method of any payment you make before a sale.

Due dates and penalties

Taxes come due twice a year, in February and July, with bills mailed in January and June. The treasurer publishes a collection timeline that shows the exact dates for each year, so check it before you set a closing date.

Montgomery County bills a full year in arrears. A first-half bill pays for January through June of the prior calendar year, and a second-half bill pays for July through December of that same prior year. Ask the treasurer which periods a pending sale touches, since that decides who owes what at closing.

  • Paying the whole year in February earns no discount.
  • Any half left unpaid after its due date draws a 10 percent penalty.
  • Halves can differ in size, because some assessments are collected on the first-half bill alone.

Payment plans and delinquent taxes

Owners with no past-due taxes can join a prepayment plan and pay in monthly installments, by mailed payment or automatic withdrawal. Enrollment closes 60 days before a due date and requires current taxes to be paid. Coupons are mailed in early March and early August.

Owners who are behind can sign a delinquent payment contract. It covers new taxes as they come due while the older balance is paid down, without added interest and penalty. A sold lien is a different case. The treasurer cannot accept payments on it, so you deal with the lien holder, and the parcel record keeps showing the lien as sold until it is formally released, even after the holder has been paid.

Other ways to pay include online, the drop box, in person, by mail and by phone.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to appeal your Dayton property value

The Board of Revision, part of the auditor's office, supplies the complaint application. To request one by mail, call 937-496-6856. ORC 5715.19 sets the deadline at March 31 of the following tax year or the end of first-half collection, whichever is later, and the treasurer describes a window from January 2 to March 31.

Complaints are investigated and may go to a formal hearing, where the owner must justify the claim. Values can rise as well as fall. The statute lets you pay on your claimed value while the case is open and gives the board 180 days after the deadline to rule on an original complaint.

A lower value can still come with a higher bill, since levies passed in your school or local district raise the effective rate. Real estate tax is shared among counties, cities, villages, school districts and special districts, and it pays for schools, police and fire protection, roads, libraries and parks.

Changing a mailing address or getting payment records

Ohio law wants a mailing-address change for tax bills in writing, and the treasurer provides a Change of Address form. A seller can file it once a closing date is set, so the next bill is not mailed to a house that has changed hands.

When a lender pays your taxes from escrow, the amount withheld shows on the lender's 1099. If you pay directly and need records, ask Taxpayer Services for an itemization, because none is mailed automatically. A bill that reaches you while a lender is responsible should go to the lender's attention, and the lender will request its own copy.

Senior and disability tax reduction

Montgomery County's Homestead Reduction Program serves owners aged 65 or older and owners who are totally and permanently disabled. Only a primary residence the owner occupies qualifies. The county homestead page has the application, so check there or call the auditor first.

The reduction also shows up at closing. Through ORC 319.202, the conveyance paperwork asks whether the seller's tax carries it, and a yes brings a sworn statement from both sides. A buyer who cannot claim it faces a higher bill than the seller paid.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Steps to take before closing

A little preparation keeps tax questions from delaying a sale:

  1. Call Taxpayer Services and ask what is owed and which half-year periods your sale touches.
  2. If any lien shows as sold on the parcel, contact the lien holder for payoff terms and ask for written proof of release.
  3. File the Change of Address form once the closing date is set.
  4. Ask the auditor whether the house carries a homestead reduction, since the conveyance paperwork will ask.
  5. If you disagree with the value and the filing window is open, request the complaint application from the Board of Revision.

The title company uses the treasurer's figures to prorate the year between you and the buyer. A cash sale moves faster than a financed one, but these same checks still apply, and a sold lien that never shows as released is the item most likely to hold up closing.

Dayton housing snapshot

Dayton was founded in 1796 on the Great Miami River. The 2020 count showed 137,644 residents, 57,751 households and 68,899 housing units, of which 16.2 percent were vacant. The ten historic neighborhoods, among them the Oregon District, Wright Dunbar, Dayton View, Grafton Hill and South Park, hold many single-family houses in styles from Craftsman to Colonial Revival.

The 1913 flood led to the Miami Conservancy District's dams and pumps, and the Memorial Day 2019 tornado outbreak produced an EF4 that crossed Dayton and nearby communities. Keep records of roof, drainage and basement repairs so a buyer can see what was done. Cash buyers often waive repairs, but documented work still supports your asking price with anyone else.

Frequently asked questions

Does the City of Dayton collect property tax?

No. The Montgomery County Treasurer bills and collects the tax, and the Montgomery County Auditor sets the value. Contact Taxpayer Services at 937-225-4010, option 1, about a bill.

What happens if I miss a Dayton property tax due date?

A 10 percent penalty applies to any first-half or second-half payment not paid in full by its due date. Call the delinquency line at 937-225-4010, option 2, to ask about a payment plan.

Why is my Dayton tax bill a year behind?

Montgomery County bills one full year in arrears. The first-half bill covers January through June of the previous year, and the second-half bill covers July through December of that year.

Can I sell a Dayton house if a tax lien was sold?

Yes, but the treasurer cannot take payments on a sold lien. Contact the lien holder for payoff terms and confirm the lien shows as released on the parcel record after payment.

How do I dispute my Dayton property value?

File a complaint with the Montgomery County Auditor's Board of Revision, which you can request by calling 937-496-6856. The deadline is March 31 of the following tax year or the close of first-half collection, whichever is later.

We buy Toledo houses as-is, and the title company pays unpaid tax from the proceeds.

Who sends the property tax bill in Toledo?

Lucas County sends it, and the city does not. The County Auditor sets the value and the County Treasurer mails the bill. Both offices are in One Government Center downtown, the Auditor in Suite 600 and the Treasurer in Suite 500. The Auditor's line is 419-213-4406 and the Treasurer's is 419-213-4305. After the Treasurer collects, the Auditor sends the money out to every subdivision in the county.

If you are preparing to sell, a quick call to each office before listing pays off. The Auditor can confirm the value, any exemption or credit on file and whether the address is registered as a rental. The Treasurer can tell you what is paid, what is open and what the payoff would be on a given closing date. Ask for both numbers in writing or by email so the title company and your buyer see the same figures.

Toledo's own Division of Taxation, in Suite 2070 of the same building, handles a different levy: the city income tax. Check the letterhead on anything that arrives. This page covers the county bill that attaches to a Toledo address.

Toledo housing in brief

Toledo has 263,423 people. Owners live in 53.3 percent of homes, the median value of an owner-occupied home is $114,500, and median gross rent is $901. With owners in just over half of homes, rentals shape many blocks. Treat those figures as a citywide midpoint, since a house in the Old West End historic district and one near the river can sit far from it. Older Toledo houses draw close looks at the roof, gutters and furnace from a buyer's inspector.

Due dates and how to pay

The bill splits into two installments, due near the end of January and again near the end of July. Ohio bills a year in arrears, so a 2025 bill is paid in 2026. A mailed payment needs a postmark on or before the date, and web or phone payments made after 8:00 p.m. Eastern wait for the next business day. Money takes 5 to 7 days to show against your parcel.

Ways to pay a Lucas County property tax bill
Payment optionHow it worksFee
OnlineDebit card, credit card or eCheck2.5 percent on cards, 50 cents per eCheck
Phone1-866-288-9803Fees apply
In personFifth floor of One Government CenterNone for cash, checks, money orders
MailEnvelope that came with the bill, parcel number on the checkNone
Drop boxSilver box at 640 Jackson Street, across from Government CenterNone
Bank branchGenoa Bank or WesBanco, January and July only, exact amount and original billNone listed

The Treasurer cautions that postmarks now usually reflect the first machine pass, which may fall a day or more after you mail the envelope. Send it early, request a hand stamp at the post office window, or pick another channel.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

The Inflation Cap Credit on your bill

It is a state-law reduction under R.C. 319.303 that appears as its own line labeled with those words. No application is needed, not every property gets it, and it is separate from both the homestead exemption and the owner-occupancy credit. The credit amount varies with property value, taxing district, school district and the taxes that qualify, and the Treasurer cannot adjust it.

Special assessments also ride on the bill after rollbacks. They cover snow and leaf removal, alleyway cleaning and sidewalk repair, among others, and they count as fees rather than taxes, so even tax-exempt parcels may owe them. Rates themselves come from levies voters passed. The basic math is 35 percent of market value multiplied by the district rate, followed by the rollbacks and credits. The owner-occupied credit and the homestead exemption apply after the House Bill 920 rollbacks.

Does the Toledo income tax matter when I sell?

It matters only if you are a Toledo filer. The city's rate has been 2.5 percent since January 1, 2021 under Toledo Municipal Code 1905.011, and individual returns are due April 15. It is a separate bill from the county's real estate tax. Appointments with the Finance Department go through Engage Toledo at 419-936-2020. Engage Toledo is also the city's request channel for tall grass, blight and structure concerns, which is worth knowing before a showing if a lot has drawn complaints.

Lucas County steps before a Toledo closing

Three county tasks come up for most sellers:

  • Rental registration. Under R.C. 5323, any livable structure that is not your primary home must be registered as a rental or carry a filed exception, with fines possible otherwise. Look up an address in the Auditor's AREIS database.
  • Deed transfer. Staff at the Auditor's office are barred from drafting a deed. The Engineer's Tax Map Department on the seventh floor approves the legal description, the Recorder checks the fee amounts, and the Auditor on the sixth floor takes the conveyance form. Both buyer and seller attend with unexpired photo ID.
  • Fees. The conveyance fee is $4.00 per $1,000 of price with a $0.50 charge per parcel, and the deed recording fee is $39.00 for two pages and $8.00 for every page after.

Mobile home titles need all current-year taxes paid before transfer.

Plan the order. Get the deed prepared by an attorney or title company, have the Tax Map Department approve the description, take the conveyance form to the Auditor, and then record. Because both parties attend with photo ID, schedule the visit around both calendars.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

When the tax on a Toledo house is behind

The Treasurer's Delinquent Installment Payment Plan lets an owner-occupant pay past-due tax over up to 24 months with 20 percent down. Plans are not issued in the ten days right after a due date. An exception request is answered in most cases within ten business days.

The county can also sell delinquent liens as tax certificates. A notice does not mean the house was sold, and the office generally keeps owner-occupied homes and homestead properties out of such sales. The Treasurer must give the record owner at least 30 days' written notice before a negotiated sale. The tax lien hotline is 419-574-6022. Separately, the Lucas County Land Bank, founded in 2010, works to return vacant and tax-delinquent properties to use.

If you plan to sell, ask the Treasurer for a payoff figure and have the title company pay it from your proceeds at closing. A cash buyer can often close quickly on a house with back taxes, but the balance still has to be cleared at settlement.

Frequently asked questions

Does the City of Toledo bill my property tax?

No. Lucas County's Auditor values the house and the Treasurer bills it. The city collects income tax through its Division of Taxation.

How soon does a mailed Lucas County tax payment post?

Allow 5 to 7 days. Timeliness turns on the postmark, and the Postal Service may stamp the envelope a day or more after you drop it off, so mail well ahead of the due date.

Is the Inflation Cap Credit the same as homestead?

No. It is automatic under R.C. 319.303 and separate from the homestead exemption and owner-occupancy credit. Your bill shows it on its own line when it applies.

Must a Toledo rental be registered before I sell it?

Yes. Rentals belong in the Lucas County Auditor's registry, and a property that is not your primary home but is not a rental needs an exception on file. Skipping it may bring fines.

What is the Toledo city income tax rate?

It is 2.5 percent, in place since January 1, 2021. It is separate from the county real estate bill.
